content: 1. Anaphylaxis and Hypersensitivity Reactions: Anaphylaxis and hypersensitivity reactions have been reported with the use of antibacterial agents, including daptomycin (CUBICIN). These reactions can be life-threatening. If an allergic reaction to daptomycin occurs, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and appropriate medical therapy should be initiated. 2. Myopathy and Rhabdomyolysis: Myopathy, characterized by muscle pain or weakness accompanied by elevations in creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal (ULN), has been reported with daptomycin use. Rhabdomyolysis, with or without acute renal failure, has also been observed. Patients receiving daptomycin should be monitored for muscle pain or weakness, particularly in the distal extremities. Weekly CPK monitoring is recommended, with more frequent monitoring in patients receiving concurrent or recent therapy with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors or those with elevated CPK levels during treatment. In patients with renal impairment, both renal function and CPK levels should be monitored more frequently than once weekly. Clinical trials have shown that CPK elevations are more common when daptomycin is dosed more than once daily; therefore, daptomycin should not be administered more frequently than once daily. The drug should be discontinued in patients with unexplained signs and symptoms of myopathy and CPK levels >1,000 U/L (~5× ULN) or in asymptomatic patients with marked CPK elevations >2,000 U/L (≥10× ULN). Temporary suspension of agents associated with rhabdomyolysis, such as HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors, should also be considered in patients receiving daptomycin. 3. Eosinophilic Pneumonia: Eosinophilic pneumonia has been reported in patients receiving daptomycin. In these cases, patients developed fever, dyspnea with hypoxic respiratory insufficiency, and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates. Symptoms typically appeared 2 to 4 weeks after starting daptomycin and resolved upon discontinuation of the drug and initiation of steroid therapy. Recurrence of eosinophilic pneumonia upon re-exposure to daptomycin has been reported. Patients presenting with these symptoms while on daptomycin should undergo prompt medical evaluation, and the drug should be discontinued immediately. Treatment with systemic steroids is recommended. 4. Peripheral Neuropathy: Cases of peripheral neuropathy have been reported during the postmarketing experience with daptomycin. Physicians should remain vigilant for signs and symptoms of peripheral neuropathy in patients receiving this medication. 5. Clostridium difficile–Associated Diarrhea (CDAD): Clostridium difficile–associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all systemic antibacterial agents, including daptomycin, and can range in severity from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Antibacterial therapy alters the normal flora of the colon, leading to overgrowth of C. difficile. This bacterium produces toxins A and B, which contribute to the development of CDAD. Hypertoxin-producing strains of C. difficile are associated with increased morbidity and mortality, as these infections may be refractory to antimicrobial therapy and may require colectomy. CDAD should be considered in all patients presenting with diarrhea following antibacterial use, even if it occurs more than two months after administration. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, ongoing antibacterial therapy not directed against C. difficile may need to be discontinued. Appropriate fluid and electrolyte management, protein supplementation, targeted antibacterial treatment of C. difficile, and surgical evaluation should be instituted as clinically indicated. 6. Persisting or Relapsing S. aureus Bacteremia/Endocarditis: Patients with persistent or relapsing Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia or endocarditis, or those with poor clinical response, should have repeat blood cultures performed. If blood cultures remain positive for S. aureus, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) susceptibility testing of the isolate should be conducted using standardized procedures. Diagnostic evaluation should be performed to rule out sequestered foci of infection. Interventions such as debridement, removal of prosthetic devices, or valve replacement surgery may be required. Consideration of a change in the antibacterial regimen may also be necessary. Treatment failure due to persistent or relapsing S. aureus bacteremia or endocarditis may be associated with reduced daptomycin susceptibility, as evidenced by increasing MIC values of the S. aureus isolate. 7. Decreased Efficacy in Patients with Moderate Baseline Renal Impairment: Limited data are available regarding the clinical efficacy of daptomycin in patients with creatinine clearance (CLCR) <50 mL/min. In Phase 3 trials for complicated skin and skin structure infections (cSSSI), only 6% of patients treated with daptomycin had baseline CLCR <50 mL/min. Subgroup analysis of the Phase 3 S. aureus bacteremia/endocarditis trial showed lower clinical success rates in daptomycin-treated patients with baseline CLCR <50 mL/min compared to those with normal renal function. This decrease in efficacy was not observed in comparator-treated patients. These data should be considered when selecting antibacterial therapy for patients with moderate to severe renal impairment. 8. Drug-Laboratory Test Interactions: Clinically relevant plasma concentrations of daptomycin have been observed to cause a significant concentration-dependent false prolongation of prothrombin time (PT) and elevation of the International Normalized Ratio (INR) when certain recombinant thromboplastin reagents are used in the assay. 9. Non-Susceptible Microorganisms: The use of antibacterial agents, including daptomycin, may promote the overgrowth of non-susceptible microorganisms. If superinfection occurs during therapy, appropriate measures should be taken. Prescribing daptomycin in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria.
